The Judges
thuh JUHJ-iz
noun (the deliverers; the biblical book)
From Hebrew shophet, a judge, ruler, or deliverer, from shaphat, to judge or govern; rendered judges through Latin judex, one who declares the law.

Biblical Definition

The Judges were the deliverers whom the LORD raised up to save Israel in the long season between Joshua and the kings, and the book that bears their name records the recurring cycle of their days. That cycle turns through four stations: sin, when Israel did evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baalim; servitude, when He sold them into the hand of their enemies; supplication, when in their distress they cried unto the LORD; and salvation, when He raised up a judge to deliver them. So it is written, "Nevertheless the LORD raised up judges, which delivered them out of the hand of those that spoiled them" (Judg 2:16). Yet each deliverance proved only a respite, for when the judge was dead the people corrupted themselves more than their fathers (Judg 2:19), and the spiral ran downward through Othniel, Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah, and Samson to the chaos of the closing chapters. The book diagnoses the root of the disorder twice over: "In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Judg 21:25). This dictionary confesses that the Judges display both the patience of God toward a covenant-breaking people and the misery of men left to their own self-rule, and that they cry out for the true King, the Lord Jesus Christ.

Webster 1828 Definition

The deliverers God raised up between Joshua and the kings, whose era ran the recurring cycle of sin, servitude, supplication, and salvation. The book closes with Israel in chaos, for there was no king and every man did what was right in his own eyes.

expand to see more

THE JUDGES, noun. The deliverers the LORD raised up to save Israel from its oppressors before the days of the kings.

Their age turned in a cycle of sin, servitude, supplication, and salvation, ever spiraling downward.

"Nevertheless the LORD raised up judges, which delivered them out of the hand of those that spoiled them" (Judg 2:16).

The cycle required of Israel repentance, and met with the LORD's patient raising up of a deliverer.

Its closing sanction is the verdict that without a king every man did that which was right in his own eyes.

Key Scripture

Judg 2:16 — "Nevertheless the LORD raised up judges, which delivered them out of the hand of those that spoiled them."

Judg 2:19 — "And it came to pass, when the judge was dead, that they returned, and corrupted themselves more than their fathers, in following other gods to serve them, and to bow down unto them; they ceased not from their own doings, nor from their stubborn way."

Judg 3:9 — "And when the children of Israel cried unto the LORD, the LORD raised up a deliverer to the children of Israel, who delivered them, even Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother."

Judg 21:25 — "In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes."

Modern Corruption

The age of the Judges faces no postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that self-rule apart from God's King ends in moral chaos, while God's patient deliverances point to Christ.

expand to see more

The book of Judges holds up a mirror to fallen human nature: a people who will not keep covenant, who forget their Deliverer as soon as the pressure lifts, and who corrupt themselves more deeply with each turn of the wheel. The deliverers themselves — Gideon, Jephthah, Samson — were flawed and sometimes grievously so, that the glory of every salvation might be seen to belong to the LORD who raised them, and not to the men.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the refrain of the book itself: where there is no king, every man does that which is right in his own eyes, and the end is anarchy and outrage. This is the autonomy of fallen man laid bare, the doing of what seems right to the self in the place of submission to the revealed will of God. The patient deliverances of the era teach the mercy of God, and the closing chaos teaches the need of the true King, whom the LORD has set upon His holy hill, the Lord Jesus Christ.

Hebrew Roots

A judge in Israel was a deliverer and ruler raised by God, not merely one who decides cases at law.

expand to see more

Shophet — Hebrew for a judge, ruler, or deliverer, from shaphat, to judge and govern.

Judge — through Latin judex, one who declares and administers the law.

The judges were charismatic deliverers, raised for a season to break an oppressor's yoke.

The recurring cycle ran sin, servitude, supplication, salvation, then relapse and a deeper fall.

The book's refrain — no king in Israel — frames the era as the misery of self-rule awaiting the true King.

Usage

"The age of the Judges ran the weary cycle of sin, servitude, supplication, and salvation."

"Whenever Israel cried unto the LORD, He raised up one of the Judges to deliver them."

"The book of the Judges ends in chaos, for there was no king and every man did right in his own eyes."
